question: What is 'Copilot for Sales' and who is it designed for?
options: A tool for creating animated sales presentations with AI-generated visuals and automatic transition effects
A specialised Copilot add-in for sales teams that surfaces CRM data from Salesforce or Dynamics 365 in Outlook and Teams to help sellers prepare for calls, draft emails, and update records
A pricing optimisation engine that uses AI to recommend personalised discounts based on individual customer history
A Microsoft Store product that helps retail employees answer product questions on the shop floor using a tablet
explanation: Copilot for Sales integrates CRM context into the productivity tools sellers already use — so when emailing a customer, they see account history, open opportunities, and can push meeting notes back to the CRM without leaving Outlook.

question: In a customer service AI agent, what is the 'escalation path' and why must it be designed before deployment?
options: A feature that automatically increases the agent's capability tier when incoming requests become too complex for its current level

A pre-defined route for transferring a customer to a human agent when the AI cannot handle the case — including triggers, handoff data, and wait-time communication — so customers are never left in a dead end
A performance optimisation system that routes requests to faster servers during peak demand periods throughout the day
A pricing tier upgrade path triggered when a customer's account reaches enterprise-level usage thresholds in the system
explanation: Every AI agent deployment must answer: what happens when the AI fails? The escalation path — when, how, and to whom a case transfers — must be designed upfront. A missing escalation path turns AI errors into customer service failures.

question: What is a 'delimiter' in a prompt, and why is it useful?
options: A special character used to end every prompt so the AI knows you have finished typing your request
Markers like triple quotes or XML tags that clearly separate different sections of a prompt — such as your instructions from the document you want the AI to analyse
A word count limit you include at the top of a prompt to prevent the AI from generating overly long responses
A type of prompt that limits the AI to responding only with simple yes or no answers to your question
explanation: Delimiters — like triple backticks, <document> tags, or dashes — make prompt boundaries unambiguous. They prevent the AI from confusing your instructions with the content you want it to process.

question: Claude is asked to write code and then run it. Which Claude feature makes this possible?
options: Extended Thinking mode, which allows Claude to simulate code execution within its internal reasoning steps
Claude Code, Anthropic's CLI agent that can actually write and execute code in your local environment via the terminal
The Artifacts panel, which has a built-in JavaScript runtime that can execute any code Claude generates
Claude cannot execute code under any circumstances — it can only write code for the user to run manually
explanation: Claude Code is the agentic tool that takes Claude out of chat and into your terminal — it can read files, write code, run tests, and iterate based on results in your actual development environment.

question: Why should an AI agent prefer 'reversible' actions over 'irreversible' ones when both achieve the same goal?
options: Reversible actions are always faster to execute and consume fewer computational resources during processing
If a reversible action turns out to be wrong, it can be undone — limiting the damage. An irreversible mistake may be impossible or very costly to correct after the fact
Regulatory frameworks require reversibility for any AI action taken in a commercial production context
Reversible actions never require human approval, while irreversible actions must always be confirmed manually by a supervisor
explanation: Preferring reversibility is a safety principle: move a file to trash rather than delete permanently; stage a draft rather than publish. This keeps mistakes recoverable while preserving the ability to course correct.

question: What is Microsoft Designer and how does it relate to Copilot?
options: Microsoft Designer is the new name for Microsoft Paint, updated with AI-powered drawing assistance tools
Microsoft Designer is an AI-powered graphic design tool that uses Copilot capabilities to help users create images, social media graphics, and visual content from text descriptions
Microsoft Designer is a tool for creating database schemas and entity relationship data models with AI assistance
It is a project management view in Microsoft Project that uses AI to suggest optimal resource assignments for teams
explanation: Microsoft Designer is an AI-first design tool in the M365 family — it generates images, posters, social posts, and more from natural language prompts using the same Copilot AI infrastructure as other M365 apps.

question: What is 'agent evals' and why is it important before deploying an AI agent to production?
options: Performance benchmarks that compare different AI vendors to select the most cost-effective option for your specific use case

A systematic evaluation process that tests agent behaviour across many scenarios — including edge cases, adversarial inputs, and failure modes — to measure reliability and surface problems before real users are affected
Annual employee performance evaluations for the AI engineering team that built and maintains the agent
A code review process where agent logic is manually inspected line by line for security vulnerabilities by senior engineers
explanation: Agent evals are your quality gate: they run the agent against diverse test cases — happy paths, edge cases, and adversarial inputs — measuring accuracy, safety, and failure rate before production. Skipping evals means discovering problems on real users.

question: What is the most effective way to ask an AI to critique your own work?
options: Simply ask 'what do you think?' and let the AI assess whatever aspects it finds most relevant
Specify the criteria for evaluation — the goal of the piece, the intended audience, and which specific aspects you want feedback on — so the critique is focused and actionable
Ask the AI to be 'brutally honest' without further guidance to ensure the harshest possible but useful feedback
Provide only positive framing to get the AI into an agreeable mindset before transitioning to asking for critique
explanation: Targeted critique prompts — 'evaluate this proposal against these criteria for a technical audience' — produce specific, useful feedback. Open-ended requests produce generic observations that are hard to act on.

question: What is Anthropic's 'responsible scaling policy' and why does it matter?
options: A data centre energy efficiency programme that limits compute growth to match available renewable energy capacity
A formal commitment to pause or limit model capability increases if evaluations reveal that a model poses serious safety risks — tying capability advancement to verified safety thresholds
A policy restricting how fast Anthropic can hire new staff to ensure quality control during rapid model development cycles
A pricing escalation schedule that increases API costs as model capabilities improve in order to fund ongoing safety research
explanation: The responsible scaling policy (RSP) makes Anthropic's safety commitments concrete: before deploying or training a model above certain capability thresholds, safety evaluations must pass — tying business decisions to safety outcomes.

question: What is 'Copilot in Viva' and what problem does it solve?
options: An AI assistant for Viva Video that automatically edits and adds captions to recorded training content

Copilot integrated into Microsoft Viva employee experience apps — helping with learning, goal tracking, wellbeing nudges, and manager insights — to reduce manual effort in HR and people management workflows
A real-time translation tool for multinational teams embedded in the Viva Connections intranet portal
A compliance monitoring tool that automatically scans employee communications for policy violations and reports them to HR
explanation: Microsoft Viva covers employee experience — engagement, learning, wellbeing, and performance. Copilot in Viva adds AI to these workflows: drafting goals, summarising engagement data, and helping managers write meaningful feedback.

question: Why is it important that an AI agent tells you what it plans to do before taking an irreversible action?
options: It allows the AI to build conversational rapport with the user by demonstrating transparency before proceeding
It gives you the chance to catch a misinterpretation of your goal and stop a potentially harmful action before it happens
Regulations require all AI systems to narrate their planned actions for accessibility purposes before execution
It helps the AI train itself over time by receiving your confirmation as a positive reinforcement signal
explanation: Pre-action disclosure is a key safety pattern: if the agent says 'I'm about to delete 50 files — shall I proceed?' you can catch misunderstandings before they become costly mistakes.

question: What is 'prompt chaining' and when should you use it instead of a single long prompt?
options: A technique for linking prompts to external databases so the AI can retrieve more information automatically on demand

Breaking a complex task into sequential steps where each AI output becomes the input for the next prompt — useful when different stages require different reasoning or when intermediate results need to be checked before proceeding
A security feature that chains multiple authentication prompts to verify a user's identity before the AI responds to sensitive requests
A billing optimisation where you connect multiple short prompts to share a context window and reduce total token cost per session
explanation: Prompt chaining lets you decompose complex workflows: extract → validate → transform → format, with human or automated checkpoints between stages. More reliable than asking one long prompt to do everything.

question: When choosing between Claude's 'Sonnet' and 'Haiku' model tiers for a simple task, what is the key consideration?
options: Haiku writes in verse while Sonnet writes in prose — the choice depends on your output format preference
Haiku is faster and cheaper, making it well-suited for simple, high-volume tasks where you don't need maximum capability
They are the same underlying model running at different speeds — Haiku is just a throttled version of Sonnet
Sonnet is the default for all tasks; Haiku is only available to developers through the API and not in Claude.ai
explanation: The Haiku tier optimises for speed and cost — ideal for classification, simple Q&A, or high-volume tasks where Sonnet capability would be overkill. Matching model tier to task complexity saves money without sacrificing quality.

question: What does 'oversharing' risk mean in the context of Microsoft 365 Copilot, and what should admins do about it?
options: Users might accidentally attach the wrong file to a Copilot-drafted email — admins should disable file attachments within Copilot interactions entirely

Copilot may surface content that users technically have access to but shouldn't practically see — such as HR documents accessible via broad group permissions. Admins should audit and tighten permissions before enabling Copilot
Copilot shares usage telemetry with Microsoft too broadly — admins should opt out via the Microsoft 365 privacy dashboard settings
Users sharing their Copilot prompts with colleagues may inadvertently expose sensitive queries — admins should make all prompts private and non-shareable by default
explanation: Copilot surfaces content that users have access to — but many M365 environments have overly broad permissions. Before enabling Copilot, admins should run a permissions audit to ensure users can only access what they should.

question: What does 'scope creep' mean in an AI agent deployment, and how can it be prevented?
options: The tendency for agent response times to gradually increase as the system handles more accumulated requests over time

An agent gradually taking on tasks beyond its original design as users discover it can handle more — which can introduce unreviewed risks. Prevented by clearly defining and enforcing what the agent is and is not authorised to do
A security vulnerability where the agent silently accesses files and systems outside its designated operational folder on the server
The accumulation of unused tool integrations that progressively slow the agent down — prevented by removing tools the agent no longer uses
explanation: Users naturally push agents toward new tasks. Without clear authorisation boundaries, scope creep introduces unreviewed risks — an agent trusted with email drafts might end up sending messages autonomously. Define boundaries explicitly.

question: What is the best approach when you are not happy with an AI's first response?
options: Start a completely new conversation from scratch and ask the exact same question again hoping for a different result
Refine your prompt with additional context, clarify what was missing or wrong, and ask the AI to try again with the new guidance
Report the response as incorrect so the AI can learn from its mistake and improve immediately
Ask a completely different question and hope the AI figures out what you originally intended from context
explanation: Iterative prompting is more effective than restarting: tell the AI what was wrong or missing, and give it specific guidance to improve. The AI uses your feedback within the conversation to produce a better next attempt.

question: What is Claude's approach when it is uncertain about the answer to a factual question?
options: Claude always provides a definitive answer to avoid appearing unhelpful or uninformed to the user
Claude is designed to express uncertainty, flag the limits of its knowledge, and suggest where to verify — rather than confidently asserting something it isn't sure about
Claude refuses to answer any question it cannot answer with complete certainty and verified sources
Claude provides three possible answers ranked by plausibility and asks the user to select which sounds most correct
explanation: Honesty about uncertainty is a core Claude principle. Rather than confabulating a plausible-sounding answer, Claude is designed to acknowledge what it doesn't know and indicate where you should seek authoritative information.

question: What does 'Copilot in Microsoft Loop' enable?
options: A circular progress indicator that shows users exactly how long AI generation will take before the response arrives
AI-assisted collaborative content creation in Loop workspaces — drafting, summarising, and transforming content that all team members can then edit together in real time
A tool for creating looping animated GIFs from screenshots using the AI image generation capability built into Loop
Automated testing loops that verify Copilot output quality against a baseline before displaying the response to users
explanation: Loop is Microsoft's collaborative canvas app. Copilot in Loop lets teams generate, summarise, and refine content together — AI-generated text becomes a shared editable artifact rather than a private chat response.

question: What is 'evals-driven development' in the context of building AI agents?
options: A project management methodology where agent feature releases are gated by approval from executive evaluation panels

An approach where evaluation datasets and success metrics are defined before building the agent, then used continuously to measure whether changes improve or degrade performance — analogous to test-driven development in software
A technique where the agent evaluates its own outputs after each response and automatically refines them before final delivery
A hiring framework for AI teams that prioritises candidates with prior AI safety evaluation experience over software engineers
explanation: Evals-driven development applies TDD discipline to AI: define how you'll measure success first, build to pass those evals, and gate releases on eval results. Without upfront evals, 'improvement' is subjective and regressions go undetected.

question: What does 'autonomy spectrum' mean when thinking about AI agent deployment?
options: A Wi-Fi signal strength scale specific to AI-enabled IoT devices that operate without physical cable connections

The range from fully human-controlled (AI only suggests) to fully autonomous (AI decides and acts), with most enterprise deployments choosing a point in between that balances efficiency with acceptable risk
A performance benchmark that measures how independently an agent can complete tasks without hitting API rate limits
A regulatory framework that classifies AI systems by their level of independence for legal liability purposes
explanation: There's no single right point on the autonomy spectrum — it depends on stakes, reversibility, and trust. New deployments typically start with high human oversight and gradually increase autonomy as reliability is demonstrated.
